strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning preferences from feedback naturally expressed during conversations. The integrated pipeline and 20,281-example dataset constitute a potentially useful contribution to conversational model alignment.

Experiments cover three model families and three established benchmarks, providing evidence beyond the proposed checklist evaluation. Improvements over the starting models are substantial: Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 24.3% to 34.9%, and Arena-Hard performance from 15.4% to 32.4%.

The experimental design includes regenerated UltraFeedback baselines, expert-generated and policy-generated data variants, length-controlled evaluation, and reported separation of training and test users and conversations. These are useful methodological choices.

The pipeline is clearly explained, with detailed annotation rubrics, prompts, model identifiers, and training hyperparameters. Human validation on 50 conversations for feedback detection and 200 conversations for checklist evaluation provides useful checks on automated judgments.
weaknesses: The central claim of more accurate alignment with actual user preferences remains insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates preferred responses, filters policy-generated pairs, and evaluates outcomes. Agreement with the resulting checklists can therefore reflect shared model interpretations. Table 7 reports 57.14% agreement with humans and κ=0.372, versus 63.27% human–human agreement. Crucially, there is no comparison showing that checklists improve human agreement over unguided evaluation, nor a separate audit of whether extracted summaries faithfully capture the original feedback.

The UltraFeedback comparison does not isolate the value of natural user feedback. Prompt distributions, conversation lengths, response-pair construction, filtering, and dataset sizes differ. A control using the same WildChat prompts and comparable generation budget, but omitting or replacing the extracted feedback, would distinguish its contribution from domain adaptation and stronger-model distillation.

The 540-example test set deliberately selects common preferences and tasks resembling training examples. This supports a restricted evaluation of prevalent preferences, consistent with Section 4’s stated objective, but cannot establish broad coverage of diverse users. DSAT recall of 48.4% further limits feedback coverage. Claims about resolving bias and aligning with diverse or evolving human values exceed the evidence.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority over UltraFeedback are overstated. No confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported, and several differences are small. There are also counterexamples: Qwen-2 trained on WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66).

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful implementation details. The manuscript only promises that the dataset will be available soon and provides no release link or pipeline code. Important reconstruction details, including clustering embeddings, split identifiers, user-grouping procedures, and data-generation decoding settings, are missing. These resource-access and validation gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although the reported gains make the case close.
